population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. Gallup-style series (current use of an incretin drug for weight, AUD or 'metabolic' reasons). Current use has plateaued at ~11.5% while ever-use rose to 20%: about 13M adults started in 2027–28 and nearly as many stopped. Arithmetic: ever 20 = never-stopped 7 (35% of ever, matching ~1/3 one-year persistence) + stopped-at-least-once 13; current 11.5 = 7 continuous + 4.5 restarters; off-now 8.5 = 20 − 11.5 (of whom 1.5 had restarted once before stopping again); cycled = (4.5 + 1.5)/20 = 30% of ever-users, i.e. 6 of 13 stoppers (46%) restarted at least once, inside the parent's 36–47%/yr restart range. Age shift: 65+ up from 9% to 12% on the extended Medicare Bridge; 50–64 down from 22% to 20% as employer coverage tightened and working-age users cycled off; under-30 use is low and partly 'calm'/craving programmes on cash-pay orals. Income: bottom third rose fastest on $149–199 cash-pay pills and patchy Medicaid uptake but is still below the national figure; top third flat as some affluent urban users quit. The 8.5% off-drug group (≈22M adults) is mostly people who stopped over cost, GI effects or, since the Oct 2027 label, blunting; most have regained part of what they lost. Never-able-to-afford: about 40% of adults with obesity have never been prescribed, concentrated among uninsured and Medicaid adults in states that declined the $245 terms. Pediatric: ~0.9% of under-18s, nearly all 12–17 on injectables (no oral is approved under 18); off-label use under 12 remains specialist-only and skews to upper-income families.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge demonstration extended by CMS in Dec 2027 on unchanged terms (Medicare pays ~$245/month, beneficiary copay ~$50, BMI/comorbidity criteria) through Dec 2029; no statutory Part D obesity coverage. Medicaid at the $245 terms adopted by a minority of states (about 16); the rest cover only diabetes/CV indications. Alcohol use disorder is not a Bridge-eligible indication; Part D plans mostly deny AUD-only claims pending compendia listing.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide in ~160 countries. India: 60+ brands, injectables now ~$6–35/month. China: domestic semaglutide generics since late 2026. Canada: several generics at ~CAD 70–100/month. Cost-plus generic oral semaglutide sold in India and Brazil. US exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32.
access.note: Managed decline: TrumpRx and manufacturer-direct cash prices stepped down to $149 for oral starter doses, $199–249 for oral maintenance (incl. Wegovy 50 mg tablet at $249) and $199–299 for injectables (Zepbound vials, CagriSema at $299). Nominal list prices (~$1,000–1,349) still exist, but almost nobody pays them. Orals have made up most new starts since mid-2027 and ~40% of all current users by late 2028; injectables keep the legacy base and the highest-efficacy tier. Employer coverage for weight management drifted down from 60% to 57%, and many remaining plans now require oral-first step therapy. FDA finalised the exclusion of semaglutide/tirzepatide from the 503B bulks list in 2027; compounded volume is a fraction of its 2025 peak. Mail-order personal import of Indian generics persists at the margins. Telehealth 'calm' and craving programmes prescribe branded orals off-label to cash-pay customers.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 + amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Dec 2026)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg and 50 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: alcohol use disorder: guideline-endorsed, not FDA-labelled (ASAM focused update Apr 2027; VA/DoD SUD guideline 2028) as an option for AUD with comorbid obesity or type 2 diabetes; Novo phase 3 in AUD reading out 2029
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol use disorder without obesity: cash-pay oral semaglutide, under the guideline's 'consider' language
low-dose 'calm', 'focus' and 'food-noise' programmes for people with BMI under 30, via cash-pay telehealth
nicotine and gambling craving reduction: observational, prescribed by addiction specialists
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
switch-to-oral maintenance after injectable weight loss
drugs.pipeline_note: Applied product by product. CagriSema: under review in the parent; approved Dec 2026 (~20%), slow uptake after failing non-inferiority vs tirzepatide. Retatrutide: BLA filed Mar 2027; FDA extended review with a major amendment over the dysesthesia signal and 11% AE discontinuation; decision expected Q1 2029, so not on market. Amycretin: phase 3 since May 2026, no filing, not on market. Survodutide: phase 3 readouts 2028, no US filing in window. MariTide (monthly) and bimagrumab: still in trials, not on market. Oral parity is delivered by an existing product in a new form: FDA approved a 50 mg Wegovy tablet (Mar 2028) with ~16–17% mean loss, matching injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg in its label trial. Foundayo's label added maintenance after an injectable-to-oral switch. Parity is with injectable semaglutide, the most-used injectable. Tirzepatide (~21%) and CagriSema (~20%) are still ~4 points ahead, but for most patients that gap no longer justifies a needle. Market ~$105B globally in 2028: volume rising, net price per patient falling.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Most common class effect; slightly lower discontinuation on slow-titrated orals; still the leading cause of stopping.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; unchanged.
Absolute risk low; large pooled CVOT analyses still show no clear causal excess.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone density
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–40% of weight lost is lean mass in DEXA sub-studies; bone-density loss confirmed in older adults in 2027 cohort data; concern concentrated in 65+ Bridge enrollees.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change; geriatric society guidance recommends resistance training and protein targets; muscle-preserving adjuncts still in trials.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA added NAION to semaglutide postmarketing adverse reactions (2027); EMA 'very rare' label retained; no class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association; the 2027 anhedonia analysis also found no excess in suicidal behaviour.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning remains removed (since Jan 2026); some psychiatrists dispute the separation from the new anhedonia label.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FDA class label (Oct 2027): clinically meaningful anhedonia or emotional blunting in ~4% of patients at maintenance doses vs ~1.5% on placebo, from pooled trial AE recoding plus a prospective cohort; dose-related; most cases resolve within 4–8 weeks of dose reduction or stopping. Patient-run surveys report 10–18%. Manufacturers say 4% overstates it, and patient groups say it understates it.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Section 505(o)(4) safety labelling change across semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, CagriSema and orforglipron: Warnings and Precautions plus a Medication Guide paragraph. No REMS or monitoring requirement. Postmarketing study with validated anhedonia scales required.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Real-world pooled data converge on roughly half of lost weight regained within a year; trial figures (two-thirds) remain the upper bound.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; supports chronic-therapy framing and oral-maintenance switching.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Signals of low B12, iron and vitamin D in long-term users; stronger in low-dose users with BMI under 30.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~6 years of rigorous follow-up now exists for adults; cycling affects ~30% of ever-users with no outcome data; adolescent cohorts are too young to read.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals; NIH-funded cycling cohort launched 2027.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New reports falling since the 2027 503B exclusion; residual harms from mail-imported generics and counterfeit pens.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B bulks exclusion finalised 2027; import alerts on unapproved semaglutide.
Reason for the extended retatrutide review; not on the US market.

safety_ledger.effect: Underweight, low energy availability and disordered eating in sub-obese 'calm' or 'food-noise' users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Case series from eating-disorder clinics in Los Angeles and New York; no denominator.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households ~25% of US households; packaged snack and confectionery volumes down ~2–3% a year, offset by price/mix, protein-forward lines and smaller formats. 'GLP-1-friendly' is now a standard retail shelf tag. Most new starts are on pills, but this has not changed household purchasing.

alcohol.state: US spirits depletions down ~4% in 2027 and ~5% in 2028; brown spirits and value vodka worst hit as the heaviest-drinking decile thins after the ASAM endorsement put the drug into addiction clinics. Non-alcoholic beer and premium low-volume 'occasion' drinks growing but far from offsetting. Distillers cutting US capacity and leaning on export markets.

restaurants.state: Traffic holding; check mix shifted to smaller plates and premium items. A counter-niche of 'appetite' dining (large-format tasting menus, eat-everything supper clubs) has grown in Los Angeles and Brooklyn on the back of the anti-thin aesthetic.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists still shrinking (store closures at Torrid-type chains); mainstream re-buying at smaller sizes has peaked. In Los Angeles menswear and athleisure, cuts for muscular builds are a growth category.

fitness.state: Strength training is the growth engine: muscle-preservation programmes for on-drug members plus an 'unmedicated' strength culture in Los Angeles gyms. Cardio-centric chains lag.

insurance.state: Employer coverage for weight management 57%; oral-first step therapy and tighter BMI thresholds widespread; pharmacy trend moderating to ~8% as net prices fall. Medicare Bridge extended unchanged; the cost question was deferred to 2029, not settled.

pharma.state: Novo–Lilly duopoly intact in the US; volume up on orals, net price per patient down ~15–20% over the window. Revenue growth slowed from the 2025 forecasts. Ex-US revenue eroding under generics. Investors watch the anhedonia label for discontinuation effects, which so far are a couple of points.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: In most of the country a thin middle-aged body still reads as 'on it' and is unremarkable. In Los Angeles's commercial-casting and fitness trades, plain thinness now reads as cheap and pharmaceutical. The prized look is visible muscle, a big appetite eaten in public, and an 'unmedicated' claim nobody can verify.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: A $149 pill put drug-thinness within reach of middle-income cash payers, so it stopped marking affluence in the circles that set taste. Among LA creatives and Brooklyn professionals, high status now means a trainer, a protein budget and a body that looks earned. Lower-income adults without coverage remain the largest group never treated.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: GLP-1 households keep eating small. In LA and Brooklyn, conspicuous eating has become a performance: whole-fish dinners, second desserts, 'I eat' posts. Some of the people performing it are on low-dose pills.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Since the label, 'are you on it?' has become a second-date question in LA and Brooklyn app culture, and 'off it' and 'eats' are profile tags there. Couples where one partner is on a maintenance dose report negotiating dose holidays around anniversaries and holidays; anecdotal, but common in therapists' accounts.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite now has two meanings. In clinics it is a dial to be turned down; in some urban taste-making circles it is evidence of vitality and a scarce trait.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FDA-labelled at ~4% clinically meaningful vs ~1.5% placebo at maintenance doses (Oct 2027). Patient surveys put milder blunting at 10–18%. Telehealth 'calm' programmes do not cite either figure; they describe the effect as 'quiet'.
interior_life.framing: Three framings at once: a labelled adverse effect in the Medication Guide; a guideline-endorsed treatment mechanism in addiction medicine; and, in cash-pay telehealth marketing, a feature ('the quiet', 'freedom from craving', 'steady focus'). Manufacturers cannot promote off-label and publicly distance themselves, but they sell branded orals to these platforms through direct-to-consumer channels.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Low-dose oral programmes have a following among individual traders and software workers in Chicago and San Francisco, who pay out of pocket or from personal wellness stipends; employers neither require nor sponsor them. Users report fewer compulsive checks and less late-night drinking. A minority describe losing the hunger that drove them. There is no productivity data.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: In Nashville songwriting circles 'writing on it' is a recognised debate: some writers taper before sessions, and some say the drug ended their drinking and saved their careers. Gamers and gamblers report shorter sessions. Sour, spicy and very loud sensory products sell to on-drug users seeking a hit.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: The label lists decreased libido alongside emotional blunting. Couples therapists in large metros report 'dose holidays' as a negotiated practice; some partners describe the user as easier to live with, others as absent.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable electoral effect. The label split the administration's coalition rhetorically: MAHA-aligned commentators attack a 'sedated nation' while the White House promotes TrumpRx prices. Patient groups lobby for Bridge coverage of AUD and get no result.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and pro-speed on approvals (Wegovy 50 mg tablet, CagriSema). Safety labelling is used rather than restriction (the anhedonia class change). Enforcement focused on compounders and counterfeits, with no new action against telehealth 'calm' marketing.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Medicare Bridge extended at $245/$50 to Dec 2029; TrumpRx cash channel continues stepping prices down; Medicaid uptake left to states.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage conditioned on BMI/comorbidity, prior authorisation and oral-first step therapy. No adherence monitoring or mood screening is required by the label. AUD use is not tracked by payers because it mostly runs through cash.
state.workforce_or_military: None. The VA uses semaglutide in AUD care under its 2028 guideline as clinical practice, not workforce policy.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: US exclusivity holds while India and China export generics to ~160 countries. The price gap ($6 vs $249) is a fixture of political talk shows. Manufacturers continue trading US price steps for tariff relief and Medicare volume.

events.event: American Society of Addiction Medicine focused update endorses semaglutide as an option for alcohol use disorder in patients with obesity or type 2 diabetes, citing the 2026 Lancet RCT and the oral phase 2; FDA label unchanged and Medicare Bridge does not cover AUD-only use

FDA orders class safety labelling for anhedonia and emotional blunting across all incretin drugs, citing ~4% clinically meaningful incidence at maintenance doses vs ~1.5% on placebo, mostly reversible with dose reduction
CMS extends the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge through 2029 on unchanged $245/$50 terms; TrumpRx cuts injectable cash pricing to $199–299 and keeps oral starter doses at $149

FDA approves a 50 mg Wegovy tablet whose label trial matches injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg on weight loss; Lilly's Foundayo label adds maintenance after switching from injections; orals already make up most new starts

Cash-pay telehealth platform Stillwater Health launches 'Quiet', a $199/month low-dose oral semaglutide programme marketed for 'craving-free focus'; it reaches 180,000 subscribers by autumn without FDA or FTC action
Los Angeles commercial casting agencies begin listing 'unmedicated, athletic build' in breakdowns for fitness and food campaigns; local trade press reports talent being asked to sign attestations

open_tensions: The same reward-blunting effect is a labelled harm, a guideline-endorsed addiction therapy and a cash-pay 'calm' product, and no regulator has said which framing governs the marketing.

Pills removed the needle barrier but not the cost barrier: adoption plateaued at ~11.5% while employers retreat and the Medicare Bridge has been extended rather than settled. The 2029 cliff and Part D's statutory exclusion are unresolved.
About 30% of ever-users have now cycled off and on and ~22M adults are off-drug with partial regain; nobody knows what a decade of cycling, or adolescent use, does.
The anti-thin, 'unmedicated' ideal in Los Angeles cannot be verified, rewards muscle that drug users lose, and is already pushing demand toward muscle-preserving adjuncts that are not yet approved.
still_true: Medicare pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 beneficiary copay for eligible enrollees under the GLP-1 Bridge terms, now extended rather than replaced.
There is no FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US; brand exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32.
Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly remain the US incretin duopoly, with Foundayo (orforglipron) and the Wegovy pill on the market.
Indian generic semaglutide remains available for under $50/month and is sold in roughly 160 countries.
The suicidal-ideation warning stays removed from the Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels, as FDA requested in January 2026.

prose.headline: The Quiet Pill: America's weight drug went oral, got a warning label for joy, and found buyers for the calm
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 the incretin drugs have stopped spreading and started settling. About eleven and a half percent of American adults are on one, barely more than two years ago, although a fifth have now tried one. The flat line hides heavy traffic. Roughly thirteen million people started in the window, and nearly as many stopped, for cost, for nausea, or, since last October, because of something they read in the Medication Guide. The typical user is a woman in her fifties on a pill, paying through an employer plan that now makes her try the oral first. Older users increasingly come through a Medicare pilot that was supposed to end last December and was instead extended on the same terms.

The pill is the story of the window. In March the FDA approved a 50-milligram Wegovy tablet whose label trial matched the weekly injection most Americans had been taking. Lilly's Foundayo, cheaper to make, had already shown it could hold weight off after patients gave up their pens. Most new prescriptions have been oral since mid-2027. Tirzepatide is still a few points ahead and the strongest results remain injectable; for most patients those points no longer justify a needle. The triple agonist everyone expected is stuck in an extended review over a strange skin-sensation signal. Prices drift down rather than fall: $149 for a starter month of pills through TrumpRx, $199 to $299 for maintenance, $245 paid by Medicare. In Mumbai the same molecule costs less than lunch. No American generic exists or will until the next decade.

The other story is the label. In October 2027 the FDA required class labelling for anhedonia and emotional blunting. It cited about four percent of patients at maintenance doses against one and a half on placebo, mostly reversible within weeks of lowering the dose. Patient groups say the real figure is several times higher, and the manufacturers say four is generous. Six months earlier the addiction physicians' society had endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in patients with obesity or diabetes, so the effect now has an official name as a harm and an official use as a therapy. Distillers have watched their heaviest customers fade from the ledger. Brown spirits are down for a second straight year, and nothing is replacing that volume.

In the gap between those two documents a third framing has grown: the effect as a product. Cash-pay telehealth companies sell low-dose oral programmes under names like Quiet and Steady. They promise freedom from craving, from the phone, from the second drink. They never use the word on the label. Traders in Chicago and developers in San Francisco pay for it from their own pockets. Their employers are not involved. Neither the FDA nor the FTC has moved, and the manufacturers say they do not promote off-label use while selling the tablets at direct-to-consumer prices to whoever prescribes them.

Culture has moved, but locally. In Los Angeles casting and fitness, a thin body now reads as a drug you can buy for $149, and the bodies that win work are muscular, visibly well fed, and described as unmedicated. Some agencies ask for signed attestations. Brooklyn supper clubs sell second desserts as a statement. In Nashville songwriters argue about whether you can write on it. Elsewhere people mostly eat less and say little.

Underneath it all are the people not on it: twenty-two million who were and stopped, many regaining part of what they lost, and the uninsured and Medicaid adults in states that declined the federal terms. Then there are the teenagers on weekly pens whose parents could pay. Nobody knows what they will feel at thirty.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marcus Bell wakes at 5:10 in Columbus and takes the tablet with a sip of water, no more than four ounces, the way the leaflet says. Then he sits on the edge of the bed for thirty minutes doing nothing, which used to be impossible.

The dispatch board at the freight yard is red by seven. A driver is stuck outside Gary with a dead reefer unit. Marcus reroutes two loads, calls a broker, eats half a turkey sandwich at his desk and throws out the other half without noticing. Deshawn from the dock asks if he's still on the Ozempic. Marcus says it's the pill now, two forty-nine a month on the government site since the company dropped it. Deshawn says that's a car payment. Marcus says it's less than the beer was.

At six his daughter Kiara plays volleyball in a gym that smells of floor wax. Last year he was the father who stood up and shouted at the line judge. Tonight he sits in the third row with his hands on his knees and watches her serve. It's a good serve and he knows it's a good serve.

Afterward his brother-in-law takes him to Rooster's. Marcus orders a non-alcoholic IPA, drinks a third of it, and listens to a story about a boat.

At home Tasha is in bed with the medication leaflet from the drawer, folded open to a paragraph she has underlined.

"Do you feel things?" she says.

"I feel fine."

"That's not what I asked."

He turns off the lamp, and after a while he says, "Her serve was good."
